title: The four books of the Shia
word: The four books of the Shia
hookLine: al-Kafi, Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih, Tahdhib and Istibsar, with their own science of grading

lines: ONE OF A SET OF FOUR.
cards: For the one who has no jurist at hand. That's the title of a book, put into English: Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih.
Tradition says its author wrote it for people who had no scholar nearby to ask, so they could still find what they needed. It's one of a set of four.
Shia Muslims also gathered the reports they trusted, through their own chains, checked by their own scholars. Today, their shelf. The four books of the Shia.

teach.b: First, the names. Al-Kafi, the sufficient, compiled by al-Kulayni. Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih, by the scholar known as Shaykh al-Saduq.

And two by Shaykh al-Tusi: Tahdhib al-Ahkam, the refining of the rulings, and al-Istibsar, a close look at reports that seem to disagree with each other. Four books, three compilers. Second, what's inside.

teach.h: THE PROPHET, AND THE IMAMS OF HIS FAMILY.
teach.b: These books carry reports of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and also reports from the Imams of his family, beginning with Ali, whom Twelver Shia Muslims follow as the rightful guides after the Prophet.
For Shia Muslims, the Imams are a trusted channel for the Prophet's teaching, so a chain may run through Ja'far al-Sadiq, or his father, back to the Prophet himself. Third, a beginning.

Al-Kafi doesn't open with purity or prayer. Its first book is the book of intellect and ignorance: reports about reason, what it's worth, and what it's for. A collection of religion that starts with the mind.
Fourth, the grading. Shia scholars have debated how far a report can rest on the book it sits in. Some, known as the Akhbaris, trusted the four books' reports broadly.
Others hold that no book is sound cover to cover by its name alone: with their own science of narrators and their own grades, they weigh each report one at a time.

teach.h: EACH REPORT WEIGHED ON ITS OWN.
teach.b: Later scholars wrote commentaries that walk through al-Kafi report by report, judging each chain. So the habit of asking who told whom runs here too, along its own roads. Sunni and Shia Muslims keep different shelves.
Today is about this one, on its own terms.

how: Twelver Shia scholars study the four books with teachers, and a jurist weighs each report's chain and grade before relying on it in a ruling.

practice: Say each name with its meaning: al-Kafi, the sufficient; Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih, for the one with no jurist at hand; Tahdhib al-Ahkam, the refining of the rulings; al-Istibsar, a close look at reports that seem to disagree.
Then say only the four names, and see if the meanings come back.
Last, sit with where the first one begins, a book of faith that opens with the mind, and name to yourself one question you've been avoiding thinking through, without trying to solve it.
